## Paper

## Abstract

Nonporous adaptive crystals (NACs) are a new class of organic adsorbents that benefit from the ability of their crystalline structures to adaptively transform in response to specific guest molecules. Herein, a NAC with guest-induced porous gating property is demonstrated within a small organic molecule, BiPyBz. It produces two distinct crystals, the dense packing CryRod and the pore-gating CryQuad, in which the pores are opened by water. Remarkably, both CryRod and CryQuad can be used as adsorbents for gaseous iodine, with the latter demonstrating the highest uptake capacity of 3.1 g g−1 at 75 °C among all existing NACs constructed from small organic molecules. The superior iodine adsorption capacity is attributed to the synergistic effect of iodine loaded in gated pores and neighboring layers in the formed crystal. This study underscores the potential of small organic molecules as NACs for the effective adsorption and storage of guest molecules with promising real-world applications.

---

## Introduction

Nuclear energy is regarded as a key pathway for achieving a low-carbon energy transition1. However, highly toxic and mobile radioactive iodine released from nuclear waste—such as the long-lived 129I and highly radioactive 131I—poses severe threats to ecosystems and human health2–4. Therefore, developing efficient and reliable radioactive iodine adsorbents is of critical significance for the sustainable utilization of nuclear energy5,6. To date, various porous amorphous or crystalline materials used as potential adsorbents for iodine capture have been developed and exhibited great application potential7–31. Among them, nonporous adaptive crystals (NACs) are emerging adsorbents and separation materials with excellent adsorption performance32–48. The feature of NACs lies in the negligible porosity compared with traditional porous materials with large surface areas, however, the guest molecules can be adsorbed into the crystalline structures with the adaptisorption, resulting in a crystalline structural change49,50, which has the potential for the long-term storage of radioactive iodine.

Most NACs are constructed by macrocyclic aromatic compounds containing intrinsically cavity (Fig. 1a), such as pillararenes and cages, owing to their intrinsically porous structure or cavity. For example, Huang group reported a nonporous EtP6 adsorbent for iodine capture38; Chi group reported NACs of a bipyridine cage for reversible iodine capture39. However, despite the impressive performance of these molecules, their relatively complex synthesis routes and modest yields may still pose challenges to broader development in this field.

NACs based on organic small molecules can overcome this limitation. Organic small molecules offer advantages such as straightforward synthesis, good crystallinity, and strong modifiability, allowing for the convenient introduction of functionally oriented groups. For instance, Li group reported the first small-molecule NAC, TPAPyH, with solvent dimension-dependent crystallinity property, achieving excellent iodine adsorption capacity of 1.27 g g−1 40. The challenge with NACs constructed by small organic molecules lies in their lower iodine uptake performance, which is due to the insufficient exposure of binding sites caused by dense intermolecular packing, as well as the absence of an intrinsically porous structure and flexibility within the crystal. Moreover, this packing structure hinders the diffusion of external guest molecules into the crystal interior (mass transfer process)51–53. Therefore, it is promising to consider that by creating a small amount of pores to expose the binding sites in the crystalline structures, facilitating the binding with active sites and increasing the mass transfer process in the crystal, then the adsorption capacity and efficiency of NACs of small organic molecules would be significantly enhanced54,55.

The intelligent phase transition of organic small-molecule crystals under external stimuli offers a novel approach for pore-gating process56–61. The rich intermolecular weak interactions (such as hydrogen bonding, π–π stacking, and van der Waals forces) within organic small-molecule crystals endow them with high structural tunability. This allows their crystal structures to undergo reversible and precise rearrangements in response to external guest molecules (e.g., solvents)57–63. In this process, external guest molecules can initially penetrate the crystal interior, disrupting the original packing arrangement to induce a phase transition and form a novel single-crystal structure, i.e. a gating process. Notably, guest molecules entering the crystal are not simply immobilized but exist as replaceable “pore units”. When guest molecules endowed with stronger interactions or higher affinity, they can readily replace the original molecules and occupy the active sites. This dynamically exchangeable phase transition mechanism not only enables guest molecules to interact more thoroughly with the active sites but also significantly reduces diffusion resistance and accelerates mass transfer processes within the crystal, thereby effectively enhancing adsorption performance.

Herein, an H2O-induced porous gating crystal is fabricated from a small organic molecule, BiPyBz, for superior nonporous adaptive iodine adsorption (Fig. 1b). The self-assembly of BiPyBz initially produces orange emitting CryRod, and then transforms into a CryQuad with green fluorescence emission upon the addition of a small amount of H2O. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction reveals an H2O-induced porous gating transformation mechanism. In this process, water molecules from the air are adsorbed, leading to the realignment of BiPyBz molecules. Due to the molecular-level porosity of CryQuad, it can serve as a solid adsorbent for iodine. When exposed to iodine vapor at 75 °C, it achieves an iodine uptake capacity of approximately 3.1 g g−1, the highest value among NACs formed by small organic molecules. The material also exhibits exceptional thermal stability, with minimal weight loss. Further characterizations show that iodine not only occupies the pores within the crystal structure but also expands the layers, much like a sponge swelling, contributing to its high adsorption capacity. This study highlights the potential of small organic molecules in the development of innovative organic sorbents for the capture of radioactive iodine, demonstrating both their feasibility and practicality.

---

## Results

Preparation and characterizations of BiPyBz crystals
A molecule, BiPyBz (Fig. 1b), was designed and synthesized by a one-step coupling reaction, in which the pyridine motif was designed as a hydrogen or halogen bonding active site40, and the benzothiadiazole motif as an electron acceptor and chalcogen bonding site. The D-π-A-π-D molecular backbone ensures a high photoluminescence quantum yield. The synthesis details were listed in the Supplementary Information, and the obtained product was confirmed by 1H NMR, 13C NMR, and MALDI-TOF-MS (Supplementary Figs. 1–3). The UV-Vis spectrum shows two bands at 322 nm and 425 nm (Supplementary Fig. 4), the latter of which indicate the intramolecular electron transfer.

During the self-assembly process of BiPyBz in ethyl acetate, two species were found in the solution (Supplementary Fig. 5). One is the rod-like crystal with orange emission (termed CryRod, Fig. 2a), and the other is the quadrilateral crystal with green emission (termed CryQuad, Fig. 2a). After around 24 h, CryRod disappeared, leaving only CryQuad settled at the bottom of the bottle (Supplementary Fig. 5), which was stable for more than 1 month in solution. To reveal the supramolecular self-assembly pathway, in-situ monitoring of the crystal evolution process was conducted. As shown in Fig. 2b, the pre-formed CryRod was gradually dissolved into the solution over time, while the size of CryQuad simultaneously increased (Fig. 2c). Therefore, the self-assembly process of BiPyBz can be described as a competitive pathway (Fig. 2d), where CryRod represents a metastable aggregate in the off-pathway, while CryQuad serves as the thermodynamically stable aggregate in the on-pathway.

The physicochemical properties of the above two crystals were then characterized after manually collecting the bulk sample of individual crystal. In terms of emission properties, the maximum emission band blue-shifted from 570 nm for CryRod to 533 nm for CryQuad (Fig. 2e). Compared to the photoluminescent (PL) spectrum in toluene (1 µM, λ = 502 nm, Supplementary Fig. 6), CryRod displayed a larger redshift (68 nm) than CryQuad (31 nm) in the solid state, indicating that the intermolecular interaction had an important effect on the fluorescence emission energy. Moreover, the quantum yields of CryRod and CryQuad were measured to be 7.33% and 19.68% (Supplementary Figs. 7, 8) in the solid state, respectively. In addition, the fluorescence lifetime decreased from 3.74 ns to 1.50 ns (Supplementary Figs. 9, 10) during the crystalline structural transformation from CryRod to CryQuad (Fig. 2f). These data also imply the different types of intermolecular interactions in the two crystals. Furthermore, powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) patterns proved their distinct molecular packing modes (Fig. 2g), as reflected from diverse diffraction patterns.

Besides, we also investigated the thermal stability of the above two crystals by observing their fluorescence images under in-situ heating. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 11, the emission band changed from 533 nm to 570 nm when CryQuad was heated from 30 to 180 °C, and the emission color of CryQuad gradually changed from green to orange, which is similar to the emission of CryRod. However, the emission band of CryRod was maintained at 570 nm under heating, only accompanied by a decrease in PL intensity (Supplementary Fig. 12). Besides, the PXRD pattern of heated CryQuad expressed the same pattern as CryRod (Supplementary Fig. 13). These data imply that CryQuad can be recovered to CryRod upon heating. To confirm this, thermogravimetric analysis (Supplementary Fig. 14) of CryQuad revealed a weight loss of 3% in the temperature window of 120–200 °C, which means the release of solvent. To precisely determine the phase transformation temperature, differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) measurements were performed on both CryQuad and CryRod crystals. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 15, CryQuad exhibit two endothermic peaks during the heating process at approximately 120 °C and 132 °C, corresponding to stepwise phase transitions or crystal rearrangements, but CryRod shows no obvious phase transition during heating. These results are consistent with the findings from in-situ fluorescence microscopy images.

Mechanism of the crystal evolution in solution
To reveal the evolution mechanism of BiPyBz in solution, the structure of CryQuad was analyzed using single-crystal X-ray diffraction (SCXRD). As shown in Fig. 3a, b and Supplementary Table 1, the crystal of CryQuad (CCDC 2369354) crystallizes in the triclinic P-1 space group, with unit cell parameters of a = 9.3297(4) Å, b = 9.8424(6) Å, c = 19.5238(8) Å, α = 79.940(4)°, β = 87.100(4)°, γ = 70.269(5)°, in which the asymmetric unit contains two host molecules and one water molecule. The experimental PXRD pattern and the simulated pattern from the SCXRD data coincided well (Fig. 2g), indicating the purity of respective phases. Surprisingly, the dimer formed by one H2O molecule bridging the two adjacent BiPyBz molecules through hydrogen bonds (-N···H-O-H···N-, 2.08 Å, Fig. 3b and Supplementary Table 2), which is the basic building block in the crystal structure. Then, the dimers linked to each other with π···π and C-H···π interactions, forming the crystal of CryQuad. The interlayer distance was measured to be 3.63 Å (Supplementary Fig. 16), which implies nontrivial π···π interactions between BiPyBz molecules. With this stacking mode, eight adjacent pyridine groups formed a pore with a size of 8.38 × 6.07 × 5.07 Å3 (Fig. 3c and Supplementary Fig. 17). It has to be noted that CryRod is a nonporous crystal, because of the low surface area of 3.37 m2 g−1 of CryRod from the BET measurement (Supplementary Fig. 18).

Despite the metastable nature of CryRod, the high-quality crystals were obtained successfully. The X-ray structure of CryRod (CCDC 2369352) was resolved (Fig. 3d and Supplementary Table 3). Unlike the CryQuad, CryRod crystallizes in the orthorhombic Pca21 space group, with unit cell parameters of a = 22.9015(9) Å, b = 3.95360(10) Å, c = 17.7923(8) Å, in which each unit cell contains four symmetry-dependent molecules. The structure of CryRod is shown in Fig. 3d. As we expected, no bound H2O molecules were found in the crystal structure. The BiPyBz molecules are stacked by multiple hydrogen bonds (meta-H of pyridine group and N of pyridine group, 2.67 Å and 3.81 Å) and chalcogen bonds (3.21 Å) between N···S (Fig. 3d), and the interlayer π···π interactions (Supplementary Fig. 19). The distance of interlayers was measured to be 3.39 Å (Supplementary Fig. 19), which indicates a more intense π···π interaction than that in CryQuad. Compared to the structure of CryQuad, CryRod has a more regular molecular packing mode and more intense intermolecular interactions, which result in a larger redshift of emission.

To quantitatively analyze the differences in the interactions between the two crystals, the weak interactions were evaluated by the Hirshfeld surface analysis64 (Fig. 3e, f, Supplementary Figs. 20, 21). The O-H···N hydrogen bonds exhibit a significant difference, changing from 19.6% for CryRod to 13.6% for CryQuad. Moreover, the binding energy of the three hydrogen bonds in CryRod and CryQuad was calculated by DFT calculation with the Gaussian 09 package (Supplementary Table 4-5)65. The binding energy of the hydrogen bond in CryQuad is stronger (−22.12 kJ mol−1) than that in CryRod (−10.51 kJ mol−1). These results suggest that the change of the hydrogen-bonding interactions from weak to strong is the driving force for the crystalline phase transformation from CryRod to CryQuad.

Further, the influence of molecular conformations of BiPyBz in CryQuad and CryRod crystals on their emissions was considered. Supplementary Fig. 22a illustrats two distinct conformations in the CryQuad, and one conformation in CryRod crystal. These molecular conformations are similar in that they are both planar, with only minor differences in dihedral angles. DFT calculations further analyzed their differences in HOMO and LUMO orbitals. In Supplementary Fig. 22b, they have similar HOMO and LUMO values; the main difference in HOMO-LUMO gap is approximately 0.05 eV, which is insufficient to account for the emission color change from orange to green. These results suggest that the differences in the intermolecular packing mode are the main reason for the emission color change.

Based on the above analysis, the evolution mechanism of the BiPyBz aggregates can be proposed. As shown in Fig. 2d, a competitive self-assembly process of BiPyBz, kinetically controlled off-pathway and thermodynamically controlled on-pathway, is involved. In the off-pathway, the monomer rapidly self-assembles into metastable nuclei, which then assemble into metastable crystals. Over time, H2O in the solvent interacts with BiPyBz, leading to the formation of dimers through hydrogen-bonding interactions. These dimers further assemble into new thermodynamically stable nuclei, which elongate into stable crystals via a self-catalyzed polymerization process. The thermodynamically stable nuclei, having a lower energy landscape, cause the disassembly of the higher-energy metastable crystals (Supplementary Fig. 23). This disassembly is the rate-determining step of the entire self-assembly process. Therefore, the second nucleation-elongation process represents the on-pathway.

H2O vapor-induced pore-gating
The crystal transformation from CryRod to CryQuad occurred not only in solution but also in air. During the experimental procedures, we found that CryRod changed its fluorescence from orange to green upon exposure to air (Fig. 4a). To elucidate the reason for this phenomenon, the fluorescence image of CryRod was monitored in-situ at ambient conditions. The orange emission of CryRod gradually changed into green emission over time when exposed to air (T = 25 °C, relative humidity RH = 60%). Interestingly, the transformation process begins from the two sides of the crystal and gradually moves towards the center of the crystal. Emission spectra (Fig. 4b) and PXRD patterns (Fig. 4c) prove that the green-emission aggregates are the same as the CryQuad phase. Then, we consider that if the fluorescence can serve as a built-in indicator for the phase transition. The in-situ fluorescence emission spectra of the phase transition from CryRod to CryQuad were measured. In Supplementary Figs. 24a–c, the in-situ emission monitoring of the phase transition process from CryRod to CryQuad exhibited the gradual blue-shift of the emission peak from 570 to 535 nm. Furthermore, the maximum emission peak exhibited a linear relationship with the transition time under vapor exposure, reaching equilibrium at 100 h. To further determine the correlation between mass ratio and transition time, the physically mixed samples with varying mass ratios of CryRod and CryQuad were prepared. The maximum emission peaks indicate a blue shift from 570 nm to 535 nm as the CryQuad ratio increased. A non-linear correlation is observed between the maximum emission wavelengths and the CryQuad mass ratios [CryQuad / (CryQuad + CryRod)] (Supplementary Figs. 24d, e). Based on this relationship, the correlation between the CryQuad mass ratio and the phase transition time can be obtained (Supplementary Figs. 24f). These results indicate that the position of the maximum emission peak value can reveal the mass ratios between CryRod and CryQuad. This provides a quantitative optical indicator for evaluating the extent of phase transition during the vapor-induced structural evolution process.

In addition, SEM images show the morphological changes from smooth rods to rough rods, which are composed of smaller bulk crystals (Fig. 4d, e). These results indicate the successful transformation from metastable crystals to thermodynamically stable crystals in air, suggesting the occurrence of the pore-gating process. Then, the effects of humidity and temperature on the crystalline phase transformation process were also studied. According to Fig. 4f and Supplementary Fig. 25, the crystalline phase transformation can occur in a wide humidity range from RH = 60% to 100%, in which the transformation time decreases with the rise of RH. Meanwhile, the transformation time accelerated as the temperature increased, likely due to the faster molecular motion and gas diffusion at higher temperatures (Supplementary Fig. 26). Additionally, other solvents, such as dichloromethane, tetrahydrofuran, methanol, and acetic acid, were also determined that they cannot trigger the phase transition from CryRod to CryQuad (Supplementary Fig. 27).

Subsequently, the crystal structural transformation process was further investigated via simulating the crystal morphology and indexing the major crystal faces to determine the evolution pathway of CryRod. In Fig. 4g and Supplementary Fig. 28, the simulated crystal morphologies are consistent with the experimental results. The macroscopically long axis direction of CryRod is the crystallographic b-axis of the unit cell, which is different from CryQuad. The molecular packing mode in the [101] facet of CryRod and CryQuad indicated the molecular transformation mode in the crystal phase transformation. This means the crystal evolution process started along the direction of the b-axis. On this basis, the evolution process can be established at the atomic level (Fig. 4h). In the first stage, H2O molecules are adsorbed on the surface of CryRod through hydrogen bonds between the nitrogen site in the pyridine group and H2O. In the second stage, H2O molecules distributed on the [101] facet further penetrate the crystal structure along the b-axis, altering the hydrogen bonds from BiPyBz···BiPyBz to BiPyBz···H2O. This transformation to higher-energy hydrogen bonds is identified as the driving force behind the crystal evolution. In the third stage, the molecular-level pores in CryQuad facilitate the transport of external H2O molecules into the crystal interior structure through pores on both sides, ultimately causing an emission transition of CryRod toward the center of the crystal on a macroscopic scale.

Gaseous iodine adsorption
To determine the adaptive adsorption properties of CryRod and CryQuad, they were used as adsorbents for iodine vapor adsorption due to their nitrogen-rich environments in the crystal structure. The as-prepared CryRod and CryQuad were exposed to iodine vapor at 75 °C and 25 °C to evaluate the adsorption performance, respectively. The mass of iodine uptake reached up to 3.1 g g−1 and 2.8 g g−1 for CryQuad at the temperatures of 75 °C and 25 °C, with the color of the crystal changed to dark black (Supplementary Fig. 29) respectively, corresponding to ~4.2 iodine atoms per BiPyBz molecule (Fig. 5a). Notably, the iodine adsorption speed was quite high, with the iodine uptake reaching 70% of the saturated adsorption capacity within the first 2 hours. The iodine adsorption performance of CryRod reached 2.5 g g−1 and 1.8 g g−1 at the temperatures of 75 °C and 25 °C, respectively. These results indicate that CryRod and CryQuad have high adaptive adsorption properties. The higher adsorption performance of CryQuad than CryRod suggests that the pores play a key role in the adsorption process. The iodine adsorption performance of CryQuad is among the highest reported for NACs constructed by small organic molecules, even better than many porous materials, like COFs, MOFs, and so on (Fig. 5b and Supplementary Table 6).

To investigate the adsorption kinetics, the adsorption behaviors of CryQuad and CryRod at 25 °C and 75 °C were quantitatively analyzed (Supplementary Fig. 30). The results show that CryQuad follows a pseudo-second-order kinetic model at both temperatures, indicating a chemisorption-dominated process. In contrast, CryRod exhibits temperature-dependent behavior, following the pseudo-second-order kinetic model at 75 °C. At 25 °C, however, the adsorption amount increases linearly with time, suggesting a diffusion-controlled process. This behavior of CryRod is likely due to limited exposure of active sites or pores at 25 °C, caused by dense molecular packing. To determine the effect of the phase transition for the iodine adsorption performance directly, the iodine adsorption experiments of both phases coexisting were incorporated, in which the samples were obtained at different phase transition times. In Supplementary Fig. 31, the iodine adsorption capacity exhibited an increase at both 75 °C and 25 °C in the presence of higher CryQuad ratios [CryQuad / (CryQuad + CryRod)]. Especially at 25 °C, there is an observed increase in the saturated iodine adsorption capacity, as well as a concomitant decrease in the adsorption time. These findings also suggest that the H2O-gated pores in CryQuad facilitate iodine adsorption by providing accessible channels for molecular diffusion and interaction.

To elucidate the reason for the high adsorption capacity, the iodine adsorption process of a single crystal of CryQuad was monitored in-situ by a fluorescence microscope at 25 °C. In Fig. 5c, with increasing adsorption time, the crystal size of CryQuad enlarged from 16.6 μm × 17.1 μm to 21.4 μm × 18.2 μm in length and width (Fig. 5c) at 120 min, and the emission intensity showed an exponential decay in 30 min without emission peak shift (Supplementary Fig. 32). Meanwhile, the crystal color of CryQuad turned from yellow to dark black, and the emission was gradually quenched by the adsorption of iodine. SEM images of CryQuad and I2@CryQuad demonstrated the structural expansion and cracking after the iodine adsorption (Fig. 5d, e). Notably, Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping demonstrated that iodine is homogeneously distributed in the CryQuad (Fig. 5f). The significant crystal expansion and the structural changes indicated that iodine is not only absorbed via the pores in the crystal but also through the synergistic effect between layers, which is the underlying reason for the high iodine capacity.

The recycle adsorption performance of CryQuad was also evaluated. After four successive adsorption-desorption cycles with DMF washing methods, CryQuad retained >77% of the original iodine uptake capacity (Fig. 5g). The PXRD pattern of I2@CryQuad remains similar before and after desorption (Supplementary Fig. 33), which confirms iodine has a strong interaction with BiPyBz. 40 The decrease in the adsorption capacity during recycling is attributed to the iodine residue in CryQuad after desorption. Furthermore, the retention experiments were performed to verify the adsorption occurring within the porous rather than on the surface by exposing I2@CryQuad to air at room temperature and ambient pressure. The I2@CryQuad almost kept its weight at 99% for at least 7 days (Fig. 5h), suggesting the uptake originates from the strong interaction between CryQuad and iodine. The excellent iodine adsorption and high retention performance of CryQuad encouraged us to construct a device for iodine vapor adsorption at room temperature (Supplementary Fig. 34). A column filled with CryQuad powder was applied for real-time removal of iodine. Different concentrations of gaseous iodine were flowed through the adsorption column. Remarkably, the iodine concentration decreased from ppm to ppb levels (Fig. 5i and Supplementary Table 7), with an impressive removal rate of more than 99.9%.

Mechanism of iodine adsorption
The adsorption mechanism at the molecular level, including the iodine species in I2@CryQuad and intermolecular interactions between BiPyBz and iodine, is revealed by PXRD, Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy, Raman spectroscopy, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). PXRD patterns (Fig. 6a) show that the crystal structure changes after the saturated iodine adsorption of CryQuad, suggesting the formation of a new structure. Time-dependent PXRD patterns (Supplementary Fig. 35) exhibited the characteristic diffraction peaks of the pristine crystal phase gradually weakened and eventually disappeared as adsorption time increases. Meanwhile, a weak new set of weak diffraction peaks emerged. These observations suggest a structural transformation during iodine uptake, indicating that iodine molecules progressively penetrate the crystal lattice and lead to lattice rearrangement or the formation of a new iodine-coordinated phase. FTIR spectra (Fig. 6b) confirmed the intermolecular interactions between BiPyBz and iodine. The intensity of characteristic peak at 1660 cm−1, assigned to the C=N stretching vibration of pyridine groups, decreased after iodine adsorption26, which indicate the halogen bonding interactions between iodine and BiPyBz. Raman spectra (Fig. 6c) show two new bands appearing at around 114 cm−1 and 164 cm−1 of I2@CryQuad, respectively. The band located at 114 cm−1 is assigned to the symmetric stretching vibration of I3−. The band located at 164 cm−1 is associated with the asymmetric stretching vibration of polyiodide I3− and the symmetric stretching vibration of I5−. The complex of Py···I2 based on halogen bonding interaction ionizes into [Py···I]+ cation and I− anion66. Furthermore, the I− anion combines with one or two iodine molecules to form I3− and I5− anions (Supplementary Fig. 36). This is the reason iodine exists in the form of I3− and I5− in I2@CryQuad, and forms a charge-transfer complex with BiPyBz. Furthermore, XPS spectra were used to identify the form of iodine in I2@CryQuad. In Fig. 6d, signals located at 617.57 and 629.03 eV are assigned to I3−, and signals at 622.49 and 634.04 eV are assigned to I5−. Moreover, the N 1s orbital peak at 397.98 eV for the C=N bond in CryQuad shifted to 399.46 eV (Supplementary Fig. 37), indicating the formation of quaternary ammonium cations (N+). Therefore, the iodine adsorption mechanism of CryQuad is attributed to the charge transfer interaction between N+ and iodine anions (I3− and I5−)25.

To deeply understand the interactions between BiPyBz and I2, the crystal of BiPyBz-I2 (CCDC 2477064, Supplementary Table 8) was grown in a DMSO/H2O mixture solvent. It should be noted that the crystal structure of BiPyBz-I2 is not the same as the iodine-saturated I2@CryQuad. This is due to the differences in their PXRD patterns (Supplementary Fig. 38). It crystallizes into the triclinic P-1 space group, with unit cell parameters of a = 9.3353(4) Å, b = 10.2543(7) Å, c = 14.5105(8) Å, α = 72.809(5)°, β = 87.982(4)°, γ = 62.972(5)°. The structure of BiPyBz-I2 is shown in Fig. 6e, f. One BiPyBz molecule combined with two iodine molecules to form a supramolecule by the halogen bonding interaction. Then these supramolecules stacked in layers with a distance of 3.36 Å, indicating the π-π interactions. The distance between N of the pyridine group and the I atom was measured at about 2.39 Å, suggesting an intense halogen bonding interaction. The binding energy of the halogen bonding interaction was calculated at about −36.40 kJ mol−1 by DFT calculation (Fig. 6g, Supplementary Table 9)65. This is stronger than the binding energy of hydrogen bonding in BiPyBz-H2O (−22.12 kJ mol−1), suggesting that iodine can displace H2O in the CryQuad and fully occupy the pores.

The results of the Atomistic molecular dynamics (MD) simulation using the general AMBER force field (GAFF) confirmed the replacement of H2O. A molecular cluster containing 14 BiPyBz molecules, 2 H2O molecules, and 700 I2 molecules (the ratio of BiPyBz:I2 = 1:50) was filled in a box of 10 × 10 × 10 nm3. As shown in Fig. 6h, the I2 molecules gradually aggregated into the BiPyBz molecular cluster, and the size of the cluster expanded with the running time elongation. Notably, the H2O molecule was released during the iodine adsorption process. Thus, the adsorption mechanism is illustrated in Fig. 6i. The iodine molecules were adsorbed and filled into the pores through the electrostatic interaction and halogen bonding, replacing the bound H2O. Once the pores are filled, iodine induces an adaptive expansion of the crystal layers to accommodate more iodine.

## Methods

Materials
4,7-dibromobenzo-2,1,3-thiadiazole, 4-vinylpyridine, palladium acetate (Pd(OAc)2), sodium acetate (NaOAc), tetrabutylammonium bromide (n-Bu4NBr), and iodine were purchased from Energy-chemical company. These compounds are used as received. The solvents of N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF), chloroform (CHCl3), acetonitrile, ethyl acetate (EA), tetrahydrofuran (THF), and dichloromethane (DCM) were bought from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd., China.

Instruments and methods
NMR spectroscopic data were measured using the spectrometers Bruker AV 400. For 1H and 13C NMR spectra, chemical shifts were calibrated to the solvent lock signal (CDCl3). MALDI-TOF-MASS spectra were measured using a BRUKER microflex mass spectrometer. UV-vis absorption spectra were obtained using a Hitachi U-2910. PL spectra of monomers and aggregates were measured with a Hitachi F-4700. The samples of aggregates were prepared by spreading the aggregates on the glass substrates. Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) patterns were performed using a PAN alytical X’Pert PRO instrument (40 kV, 200 mA). Fluorescence quantum yields and Fluorescence lifetimes were measured with a FLS1000 photoluminescence spectrometer. SEM images were obtained on a Hitachi S-8010 field-emission microscope where the accelerating voltage and the current were set as 10 kV and 10 μA, respectively. Fluorescence microscope images were obtained on an inverted fluorescence microscope (Nikon Ti-2). The fluorescence microscope samples were prepared by spreading the aggregates onto the glass substrates. BET spectra were measured with ASAP 2460 Accelerated Surface Area and Porosimetry System. FTIR spectra were measured with a Bruker ALPHA II Compact FT-IR Spectrometer. Raman spectra were measured with LabRam HR Evolution. XPS spectra were measured with Thermo ESCALAB 250XI. ICP-MS data were measured with Agilent 7800. The samples that flowed out of the columns were collected with 0.3 M of sodium hydroxide solution. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction data were collected with a Bruker Apex Smart CCD diffractometer with graphite-monochromated Cu Kα (λ = 1.54184 Å) radiation at 170 or 180 K. All non-hydrogen atoms were refined with anisotropic displacement parameters, while the hydrogen atoms attached to carbons were placed in idealized positions with isotropic thermal parameters. Variable temperature fluorescence spectra were obtained using an Ocean Optics USB4000 fluorometer with a 385 nm LED lamp as the light source. The samples were prepared by spreading the aggregates on the glass substrates.

Synthesis of BiPyBz
4,7-bis((E)-2-(pyridin-4-yl)vinyl)benzo-2,1,3-thiadiazole (BiPyBz)67. A mixture of 4,7-dibromobenzo-2,1,3-thiadiazole (2.94 g, 10 mmol), 4-vinylpyridine (2.10 g, 20 mmol), Pd(OAc)2 (50 mg, 0.2 mmol), NaOAc (4.10 g, 50 mmol), n-Bu4NBr (0.65 g, 2 mmol), and DMF (50 mL) was heated at 100 °C with stirring. After reacting for 24 hours, deionized water was added to quench the reaction. The resulting precipitate was filtered and washed with deionized water to remove the DMF residue. The product was then purified by column chromatography on silica gel using ethyl acetate as the eluent, yielding BiPyBz (0.86 g, 2.5 mmol, 17% yield). 1H NMR (400 MHz, CDCl3) δ 8.65 (d, J = 5.9 Hz, 4H), 8.05 (d, J = 16.3 Hz, 2H), 7.84–7.74 (m, 4H), 7.52 (d, J = 5.8 Hz, 4H). 13C NMR (101 MHz, CDCl3) δ 153.74, 150.36, 150.32, 144.60, 131.42, 129.32, 128.68, 128.43, 121.11. Calcd. for BiPyBz: m/z [M-H]− = 341.4. Found: MALDI-TOF-MS: [M-H]− = 341.85.

Fabrication of BiPyBz aggregates
10 mg BiPyBz solid was added to 2 mL ethyl acetate solution, and heated to dissolve completely. CryRod was formed by cooling the solution to room temperature with orange emission. Then, it was transformed into CryQuad with green emission after 24 hours. The transformation cannot occur when the supra-dried ethyl acetate was used.

Iodine vapor uptake capacity
The procedure for static iodine vapor sorption was performed as follows: the crystal (CryQuad or CryRod, 10 mg) was placed in a vial (4 mL), then the vial was placed in a large wide-mouth bottle (20 mL) containing iodine. The bottle was sealed and kept at 25 °C or 75 °C. The weight of the small vial was measured periodically, until reaching the equilibrium.

In-situ iodine adsorption of CryQuad
The in-situ iodine adsorption of CryQuad was obtained by putting CryQuad and a small dish (1 cm in diameter) containing iodine into a culture dish (2 cm in diameter) with a glass bottom, sealed with sealing film, and observed under a fluorescence microscope.

Adsorption kinetics
The adsorption kinetics were quantified using Ho and McKay’s pseudo-second-order model, from which the apparent rate constant kobs can be calculated using the following equation:
t/qt = 1/(kobs × qe2) + t/qe (1)
where qt and qe are the adsorbate uptakes (g adsorbate per g adsorbent) at time t (h) and at equilibrium, respectively, and kobs is an apparent second-order rate constant (g g−1 h−1). The rate constant kobs can be calculated from the intercept and slope of the plot of t/qt against t.

Recycle adsorption
50 mg of I2@CryQuad solid was added to a 20 mL DMF solution and subjected to ultrasound for 1 h to induce iodine desorption. The resulting sample was filtered and washed with methanol and excess water before being dried. The sample was then used for iodine uptake again.

The adsorption performance of the column filled with CryQuad
CryQuad (50 mg) was filled into the column with a length of 8.5 cm, and the ends of the column were filled with cotton. Injecting 10 mL iodine vapor (concentrations of 3000 ppm, 1500 ppm, and 300 ppm, respectively) into the column at a rate of 3.3 mL/min, and the output gas was absorbed with 0.3 M sodium hydroxide solution (10 mL). The iodine concentration in the solution was detected by ICP-MS, and the iodine concentration (cvapor) of the output gas was calculated with the equation as follows:
cvapor = (csolution × Vsolution) / Vvapor (2)
where csolution is the iodine concentration in solution, measured by ICP-MS; Vsolution is the volume of the sodium hydroxide solution, 10 mL; Vvapor is the volume of iodine vapor, 10 mL.

Theoretical calculations
The density functional theory (DFT) calculation processes were carried out using the Gaussian 09 software package65. The imported BiPyBz molecular structure was derived from the single crystal X-ray diffraction analysis with further geometry optimizations for calculating the molecular orbitals. The gas-phase ground state calculations were performed at B3LYP/6-311g* for BiPyBz and H2O, and B3LYP/def2tzvp level for I2. The electrostatic potential (ESP) surfaces were mapped for all molecules using GaussView 5.0, with the isovalue of 0.0004. The H-bond interactions between BiPyBz and H2O were performed at m062x/def2tzvp with BSSE correction using the SCXRD geometry without further optimization. The halogen bonding interactions between BiPyBz and I2 were performed at m062x/def2tzvp with BSSE correction.

The molecular dynamics simulations were carried out using the Gromacs 2018.8 program with general Amber force fields (GAFF)68. All the molecules were put into a cubic box with a side length of 10 nm using packmol software69 (700 I2 molecules for 14 BiPyBz molecules). The cutoff for the neighbor list of the Verlet method and that for short-range interactions is 1.0 nm in all calculations with periodic boundary conditions in all three directions. After the energy minimization, the systems were run in the NVT ensemble for 1 ns at 298.15 K. The time step of each simulation was 1 fs.
